replacement.title: Reset behind the blue line
replacement.objective: Use a practice reset location while separating it from a formal rule judgement.
replacement.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x). F1 owns the puck on the neutral-zone side of the right blue line. YOU are on its attacking-zone side; F2 is farther toward centre ice and D1 is farther toward the right net. The coach asks YOU to reset to the neutral-zone side before the next rep.
cues: The coach has stated a practice reset.
YOU start on the attacking-zone side of the right blue line.
This practice instruction is separate from a formal offside decision.

sources.title: USA Hockey: Skill Progressions for Youth Hockey
sources.use: Lists skill/team topics; Canadian adaptation and answers remain experimental.

replacement.limits: Static experimental practice scene. Positions are examples and do not prove timing, execution, possession outcome, or a universal team system; coaching responses are ungraded.

questions.prompt: Where are YOU relative to the right blue line in this practice?

options.text: On the attacking-zone side, toward the right net
On the neutral-zone side, toward centre ice
At the left goal line

questions.explanation: YOU are on the attacking-zone side of the blue line. The reset asks YOU to return to its neutral-zone side.

questions.prompt: Which two facts determine whether the reset is ready?

options.text: The coach's stated reset instruction
Where YOU and the teammates are before restarting
A silent offside verdict from the still image

questions.explanation: The practice instruction and player locations are visible cues. A formal call needs more timing information than this freeze.

questions.prompt: Arrange the stated reset steps.

options.text: Hear the reset instruction
Move behind the blue line under control
Re-check F1 before starting again

questions.explanation: The sequence follows the coach instruction and checks the carrier before the next action.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an example reset point behind the right blue line.
questions.explanation: This example is on the neutral-zone side of the right blue line. It satisfies the stated location, but the restart still requires the coach’s cue and a check of the other players.

questions.prompt: F1 keeps waiting after YOU reset. What is the useful next check?

options.text: Whether F1 still has a reachable route and whether the coach has restarted the rep
Assume the pass must happen now
Make a full rule call from the picture

questions.explanation: The waiting changes the practice timing cue. Re-check F1 and the stated restart rather than inventing a formal ruling.

questions.prompt: What information is still missing before a formal offside decision?
questions.explanation: The coach's reset is visible, but timing and rule context are not. Follow the drill instruction and avoid treating the freeze as a formal ruling.

replacement.title: Stop the rep and reset
replacement.objective: Respond to a clear stop instruction before resuming a new puck task.
replacement.briefing: Navy attacks +x. The puck is loose between YOU and D1 when the coach stops the rep. F2 is nearby. The stop changes the task even though no player has yet touched the puck.
cues: The coach has clearly stopped the rep.
A restart may assign F2 as the carrier.

sources.title: USA Hockey: Skill Progressions for Youth Hockey
sources.use: Lists skill/team topics; Canadian adaptation and answers remain experimental.

replacement.limits: Static experimental practice scene. Positions are examples and do not prove timing, execution, possession outcome, or a universal team system; coaching responses are ungraded.

questions.prompt: What changed the task while the puck stayed loose?

options.text: The coach called stop
D1 touched the puck
F2 was assigned the puck before the stop

questions.explanation: The briefing states a clear stop call; the puck still has no owner.

questions.prompt: Which actions fit the stop instruction?

options.text: Pause the contest and listen
Follow the coach’s reset directions under control
Continue battling for the loose puck

questions.explanation: The stop call changes the task, so listening and resetting fit; the loose puck is no longer the immediate objective.

questions.prompt: Arrange this stop-and-reset response.

options.text: Hear and acknowledge the stop
Leave the contest under control
Confirm the restart cue

questions.explanation: The order respects the stated practice instruction before a new puck task begins.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an open reset point away from the loose-puck contest.
questions.explanation: This point separates YOU from the puck and D1 so the stop can be followed without another contest.

questions.prompt: The coach restarts with F2 as the puck carrier. What should YOU confirm?

options.text: F2's location, D1's pressure, and the new support job
Continue the old loose-puck plan
Assume YOU own the restart

questions.explanation: The restart assigns a new carrier, so scan F2 and D1 before choosing support.

questions.prompt: Why can the right decision change even when nobody touches the puck?
questions.explanation: The coach changed the task and the restart conditions. A player must follow the new instruction, then re-read possession, pressure, and support.

replacement.title: The strong-side outlet closes
replacement.objective: Reassess an outlet when a forechecker occupies its side.
replacement.briefing: YOU control the puck beside Navy’s net on its centre-ice side. Gold 1 is near the direct lane to W. D2 is across the middle on the other side of the net. This drill permits a reverse if its route is available; it is not an automatic instruction. Navy defends the left net and attacks the right net.
cues: D2 is across the middle from YOU.
Gold 1 is near the direct route to W.

sources.title: Developing Skilled Defencemen — Overview
sources.use: Supports the stated coaching principle. The setup, alternatives and suggested answers are original experimental coaching synthesis, not source-certified.

replacement.limits: Age adaptation and tactical alternatives await coaching review. Static setup: no skating speed, interception timing or uniquely optimal route has been validated. Positional references are examples, not scored targets.

questions.prompt: Which teammate is on the opposite side of the net from YOU?

options.text: Gold 1
D2
W

questions.explanation: D2 and YOU are on opposite sides of Navy’s net.

questions.prompt: Select two checks before using the permitted reverse.

options.text: Whether D2 is ready
Whether the first planned pass must be completed
Whether pressure can reach the reverse route

questions.explanation: The reverse is an option only if its receiver and route remain usable.

questions.prompt: Arrange a possible reverse decision.

options.text: Assess pressure near the strong-side outlet
Check and communicate with D2
Use the reverse only if that route remains available

questions.explanation: The routine supports a decision, not an automatic reverse every time pressure appears.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an example spot for protecting possession while looking toward D2.
questions.explanation: A tighter position toward the middle of the net can change the angle you present to pressure. Actual goalie and defender locations still matter.

questions.prompt: If D2 is closely marked before you release, what is sensible?

options.text: Reverse automatically because it was the original plan
Pass through D2’s marker without checking
Reassess a hold or another outlet

questions.explanation: A closed second option means another read is needed; holding may be useful if possession can be protected.

questions.prompt: Why is “the first outlet is closed” insufficient by itself to choose a reverse?
questions.explanation: A different lane and a prepared receiver must also exist. Mention pressure on D2 or time to protect the puck.

questions.prompt: What should YOU check with Gold 1 near the route to W?

options.text: Whether the direct W outlet is usable
D2 must own the puck
The puck is already in the neutral zone

questions.explanation: Gold 1 is near the direct lane to W. Check reach and movement before judging whether that lane is usable.

questions.prompt: Which two details should accompany a reverse call?

options.text: Which side D2 is on
Whether the reverse lane is open
That D2 is automatically open because Gold 1 is near W

questions.explanation: Communicate D2’s side and whether the proposed route is usable. Keep the call accurate as pressure changes.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward an example behind-net position to reassess pressure and D2.
questions.explanation: The example moves the carrier and puck behind the goal line, beside the back of the net. Recheck the net, boards and pressure; the position does not prove a safe skating or passing route to D2.

questions.prompt: Why does a closed strong-side outlet permit a reverse without requiring it?
questions.explanation: The closure removes one lane while D2’s side and pressure determine whether the reverse helps; if the reverse is covered too, protect or wait.

replacement.title: Step out of the forechecker’s shadow
replacement.objective: Create a visible receiving option for a defender.
replacement.briefing: Navy D1 has the puck. YOU are a wide support player near the blue line. Gold 1 is close to the direct passing route. Navy C is closer to the defended left net and nearer the middle. Reoffer support if a usable lane is available.
cues: Gold 1 is close to the direct route to YOU.
C is a navy inside support option.

sources.use: Supports age/topic placement only. The setup, alternatives and suggested answers are original experimental coaching synthesis, not source-certified.

questions.prompt: Who currently owns the puck?

options.text: D1
YOU
C

questions.explanation: The puck is assigned to D1, so this question is about support without possession.

questions.prompt: Which two changes might make your support more useful?

options.text: Stay hidden behind Gold 1 until the pass arrives
Show a ready stick after scanning
Adjust the receiving angle

questions.explanation: Moving and preparing can help D1 see an option; any new location still needs a lane check.

questions.prompt: Arrange a way to reoffer along this wall.

options.text: Assess Gold 1 near the passing route
Move to change the passing angle
Look back and prepare to receive

questions.explanation: The order is a suggested support routine rather than a fixed skating pattern.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a different receiving angle from D1.
questions.explanation: Coming off the boards can separate the passing route from Gold 1. Check C’s space rather than crowding it.

questions.prompt: If Gold 1 follows your inward move, which response could help?

options.text: Call for a pass without looking at Gold 1
Reoffer elsewhere or make room for C
Remain still because your first move should have worked

questions.explanation: A supporter should update the option; the first movement does not guarantee availability.

questions.prompt: How can your movement help D1 even if D1 passes to C?
questions.explanation: Explain how moving Gold 1 or clearing a route can help another teammate. Receiving the puck is not the only useful outcome.

questions.prompt: Which passing route is Gold 1 closest to?

options.text: The lane between D1 and YOU
The route from C to Navy’s net
The far blue-line exit

questions.explanation: Gold 1 is close to the D1-to-YOU route. An angle change may help, but the new lane still needs checking.

questions.prompt: Which two calls help D1 use your movement?

options.text: Say when you are clear of the shadow
Identify C’s inside support
Call “I’m open” and leave D1 to guess your new angle

questions.explanation: Communicate actual availability and C’s support position. A short clear call can work; it must match the current lane.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward the middle to compare a receiving angle from D1.
questions.explanation: The example moves YOU inward and changes the passing angle. It does not prove visibility or reception; recheck Gold 1 and C.

questions.prompt: How can movement help D1 even if the puck goes to C?
questions.explanation: Stepping off the direct lane can pull Gold 1 and open C or D1’s next route; if the defender ignores you, D1 can use the space you created.

replacement.title: Offer a short inside outlet
replacement.objective: Offer a short inside outlet for a teammate under pressure.
replacement.briefing: Navy W owns the puck in a wide lane, with Gold 1 nearby. YOU start farther up ice and nearer the middle. In this exercise, offer a short inside outlet closer to Navy’s defended left net than W, if the lane is usable.
cues: The coach assigns a short inside outlet.
W is the navy puck carrier under nearby gold pressure.

sources.section: Page 1, individual tactics and team play
sources.use: Supports age/topic placement only. The setup, alternatives and suggested answers are original experimental coaching synthesis, not source-certified.

replacement.limits: Age adaptation and tactical alternatives await coaching review. Static setup: no skating speed, interception timing or uniquely optimal route has been validated. Positional references are examples, not scored targets.

questions.prompt: What support job is explicitly assigned to YOU?

options.text: Wait at the far blue line
Pressure W as an opponent
Offer a short inside outlet

questions.explanation: The briefing assigns a short inside outlet, rather than an immediate stretch.

questions.prompt: Which two features would suit that outlet?

options.text: Enough separation from Gold 1
A route W can actually see
The greatest possible distance from W

questions.explanation: Short support needs usable spacing and a route, not just proximity.

questions.prompt: Order a support response to W’s pressure.

options.text: Read Gold 1’s approach
Move closer to Navy’s net and inside W
Prepare for a pass or another change

questions.explanation: Keep updating pressure while moving; the routine is not a rigid play call.

questions.prompt: Move YOU closer to Navy’s net than W to suggest a short inside option.
questions.explanation: A position closer to Navy’s net and inside W can offer a release while avoiding the same wall pressure. Several spots may work.

questions.prompt: If W escapes Gold 1 with secure possession, what changes?

options.text: You may move forward while remaining available
You must remain underneath for the rest of the shift
You should stop watching the puck

questions.explanation: The support distance can expand when the carrier has time; possession quality still matters.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between supporting W and skating into W’s problem?
questions.explanation: A useful option creates a different angle or time advantage instead of joining the same pressure.

questions.prompt: Which Navy teammate offers a deeper reset behind YOU if W remains pinned?

options.text: D1
Gold 1
Gold 2

questions.explanation: D1 is the deeper Navy option behind YOU, so W can have a connected reset if Gold 1 keeps pressure on the wall; if D1 is covered, hold a support angle instead of forcing the pass.

questions.prompt: Which two cues tell YOU whether to keep the short inside outlet?

options.text: Gold 1’s pressure on W
W’s puck control
D1’s old position alone

questions.explanation: Pressure and control determine whether W needs a close outlet; D1’s old spot cannot answer the immediate support question.

questions.prompt: Move YOU closer to Navy’s net than W and nearer the middle than W.
questions.explanation: The example is closer to the left net than W and nearer the middle. Recheck the passing lane and Gold 1; it does not guarantee a pressure-free outlet.

questions.prompt: What would make you leave the short-outlet position?
questions.explanation: Leave when W has secure control and a better visible lane opens, or when pressure closes your route; if W remains pinned, stay available.
